analysis.one_liner: Taxes fossil fuels and uses the money to cut Social Security payroll taxes and aid low-income energy customers.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one Democrat and one Republican, the bill was referred to four House committees, never taken up, and died without a vote when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a tax on coal, petroleum, and natural gas starting at $40 per ton of carbon dioxide content in 2020, rising over time, plus a border tax on carbon-intensive imports and a fee on fluorinated greenhouse gases. The revenue would cut the employee share of Social Security payroll taxes, add annual funding for home energy assistance and weatherization for low-income households, and pay a share to Social Security beneficiaries. While the tax is in effect, it would also suspend EPA rules that limit greenhouse gas emissions from fuels, with the suspension expiring if emissions exceed what they would otherwise have been. The bill never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people would see their take-home pay rise, because carbon tax revenue would be used to reduce the employee share of Social Security payroll taxes while backfilling the trust funds so benefits are unaffected [S2] [S3]. Low-income households would gain new, automatic annual funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (5% of the revenue) and the Weatherization Assistance Program (1%), on top of existing appropriations [S2] [S3]. Social Security and Railroad Retirement beneficiaries would receive an equal share of 10% of the revenue each year [S2] [S3]. U.S. manufacturers of carbon-intensive goods would gain protection, because similar imports would face the same carbon tax and exports would get refunds [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, low-income households, Social Security retirees

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the employee share of Social Security payroll taxes (the 6.2% worker contribution, plus the self-employed equivalent), raising take-home pay; the carbon tax revenue is appropriated back into the Social Security trust funds in an amount designed to keep the funds whole, so benefits are not cut to pay for the tax cut.

Sends 5% of the carbon tax revenue each year, automatically and on top of normal appropriations, to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program and 1% to the Weatherization Assistance Program, directly offsetting the higher energy bills the tax would cause for low-income households.
Distributes 10% of each year's carbon tax revenue equally among Social Security retirement and Railroad Retirement beneficiaries, giving seniors a direct payment to offset energy costs.

Imposes a matching tax on carbon-intensive imports and refunds the tax on exports, so U.S. manufacturers are not undercut by foreign competitors who face no carbon price and jobs are not pushed overseas.

Uses the price signal — a $40 per ton tax in 2020, growing 2.5% annually (plus inflation) any year the nation misses its emissions targets — to push the economy off coal, oil, and gas, while giving refunds for carbon that is captured rather than emitted.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and gas producers would owe the new tax, and much of it would be passed through to consumers in the form of higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices [S3]. Energy-intensive industries and large users of fluorinated greenhouse gases would face higher costs, partially offset by the border tax on imports and export refunds [S3]. The public would also give something up: while the tax is in force, EPA could not enforce its own greenhouse gas limits on those fuels, trading regulation for the tax [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: Energy prices would rise. The tax is levied on coal, petroleum products, and natural gas at the point of production, and producers would pass much of it to consumers through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity costs; the payroll tax cut and energy aid offset this for workers and low-income households, but people who pay energy bills without working or receiving benefits would bear the increase directly.

It trades away EPA regulation. While the tax is in force, EPA could not enforce rules limiting greenhouse gas emissions from covered fuels on the basis of their climate effects, and any make-up regulation would only begin after a determination — first due in 2030 — that cumulative emissions exceeded what would have happened without the suspension, with required reductions fully achieved as late as eight years after that. Anyone who trusts regulation more than a tax that a future Congress could alter would see this as a serious concession.
It locks itself in. Changing the bill's revenue-neutral structure would require a two-thirds vote of the House or Senate, binding future Congresses that might want to redirect the money.
The tax would run for a very long time: it keeps climbing until U.S. emissions fall below 20% of their 2005 level, a threshold far beyond the bill's ten-year horizon.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is a genuine swap rather than a revenue grab: nearly all the money returns to workers (through payroll tax cuts), low-income households (through energy aid), and retirees (through direct payments), with the trust funds backfilled so Social Security is not shorted. The honest costs are higher energy prices, which fall hardest at the point of purchase, and the suspension of EPA's authority to regulate fuel emissions while the tax operates — a trade intended to win fossil-state support but one that leaves the public reliant on the tax actually working. On balance the bill is structured to serve working people at the expense of fossil fuel producers, but its success would depend entirely on the tax delivering emissions cuts the EPA backstop would no longer guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to four committees; none ever took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Lipinski introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, joined by Rep. Francis Rooney of Florida — a Democrat and a Republican pairing that made it one of the few bipartisan carbon tax proposals of the Congress.

That same day the House referred it to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Rules committees; it was sent to the Social Security subcommittee on July 25 and the Energy subcommittee on July 26.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever recorded in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and gas producers are better off, because the $40-per-ton carbon tax and the border adjustment never became law; the cost fell on workers who never got the payroll tax cut and low-income households who never got the guaranteed energy assistance funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers who avoided the tax

for.name: Rep. Daniel Lipinski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and designed it to pair a carbon tax with Social Security payroll tax cuts and low-income energy aid.

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Was the bill's only cosponsor, giving it its bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, sent it to a subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or hearing.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill for the Clean Air Act provisions, sent it to the Energy subcommittee, and never scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor, but because it never reached a hearing or floor vote, there is no record of how either party would have divided.

industries.note: Coal has the highest carbon dioxide content per unit of energy, so a flat $40-per-ton tax would hit it hardest of any fuel — which is the point. The industry's interest in blocking the tax runs directly against the payroll tax cuts and energy aid the revenue would fund.

The bill taxes petroleum products and natural gas by their carbon content, though it sweetens the deal by suspending EPA greenhouse gas rules on fuels and refunding the tax on exports. The tax far outweighs that regulatory relief, so the industry would still lose — and its loss is the revenue that pays for the worker benefits.

These industries (steel, cement, chemicals and the like) would pay the tax on their fuel inputs, but the bill taxes equivalent imports the same way and refunds the tax on exports, so they gain protection from carbon leakage. The public shares both sides: protected jobs, but higher costs embedded in goods.

Refrigerant and industrial gas producers and emitters would pay a fee of 10% of the carbon price per metric ton of CO2-equivalent. The same bill suspends EPA enforcement against these gases, a partial offset, but the fee is the operative mechanism.
